paragraphs: Complex optimization methods often break a large problem into smaller updates. ADMM is a prominent example, but its individual minimization steps can themselves be expensive. Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient, or PDHG, offers an alternative whose updates are often simpler, making it attractive for statistical learning and image processing.

The practical obstacle is choosing PDHG's multiple step sizes. These parameters control how the algorithm advances, and unsuitable choices can undermine efficiency or even convergence. The paper introduces adaptive rules that tune the parameters automatically, addressing a decision that otherwise requires careful manual intervention.

The authors analyze the resulting methods mathematically and establish convergence rates. Their numerical experiments also show advantages over non-adaptive methods in efficiency and ease of use. The contribution therefore connects two concerns: retaining the simpler updates that make PDHG appealing, while reducing the parameter-selection burden that can prevent those updates from becoming a practical solver.
neurips-2015-adaptive-primal-dual-splitt.tldr: Adaptive step-size rules make PDHG optimization easier to use, with analyzed convergence rates and empirical efficiency gains.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks coordinates that describe nonlinear structure in observed data. This paper introduces LL-LVM, a probabilistic model that links the observations, their hidden manifold coordinates, and local linear maps. The model is conditioned on neighborhood relationships, so nearby points provide the organizing structure for learning.

Its central idea is to describe a nonlinear manifold through local mappings from the hidden coordinate space into the observation space. Variational optimization estimates the posterior distribution over both coordinates and maps. This gives a probabilistic form to the intuition behind locally linear embedding: preserve local geometry while discovering a broader nonlinear representation.

The probabilistic formulation also supports decisions beyond finding coordinates. It can evaluate proposed neighborhoods, select the manifold's intrinsic dimension, and extend the representation to new observations. It can additionally connect with other probabilistic models describing structure within the manifold. These capabilities make the representation part of a larger modeling framework rather than only a fixed embedding of the supplied data.
neurips-2015-bayesian-manifold-learning-.tldr: LL-LVM turns local geometry preservation into a probabilistic manifold model that supports inference, model selection, and extensions to new data.

paragraphs: Large data matrices can be represented using a selected subset of their columns or rows. The central challenge is choosing a subset that preserves the matrix well enough for subsequent analysis. This paper addresses that selection problem through an adaptive sampling algorithm designed to improve existing methods.

The proposed algorithm applies to any column-selection algorithm with a relative-error guarantee. Rather than introducing only a separate selection procedure, it provides a way to strengthen that class of methods. Its theoretical contribution is a tighter bound on approximation error, making the quality of the selected representation more tightly controlled.

The authors also demonstrate the improvement using two established relative-error column-selection algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show better results than non-adaptive sampling and earlier adaptive approaches. Together, the bound and experiments support the value of adaptation in column selection: the method improves a mathematical guarantee and produces corresponding empirical benefits when attached to existing selection algorithms.
neurips-2015-column-selection-via-adapti.tldr: An adaptive sampling algorithm strengthens relative-error column selection, with tighter approximation bounds and improvements on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Estimating probabilities over many possible symbols creates a gap between worst-case theory and practical performance. This paper asks a more distribution-specific question: how close can an estimator come to a well-informed competitor for every discrete distribution? The answer depends on precisely what information or restrictions the competitor receives.

The first comparison gives the competitor knowledge of the distribution without revealing which probabilities belong to which symbols. The second gives exact distribution knowledge but requires equal estimated probabilities for symbols observed equally often. These benchmarks make the universal near-optimality claim specific: it concerns competition against these two defined classes.

A simple Good-Turing variant has an excess KL-divergence guarantee of (3 + o(1))/n^(1/3), where n is sample size. A more involved estimator achieves a bound of order min(k/n, 1/√n), up to logarithmic factors, for k symbols. Lower bounds match the latter rate for the second comparison up to logarithmic factors; the first comparison has a different stated lower bound. The results give Good-Turing a distribution-by-distribution theoretical justification.
neurips-2015-competitive-distribution-es.tldr: Competitive guarantees explain why a Good-Turing variant estimates every discrete distribution nearly as well as two carefully defined informed benchmarks.

paragraphs: Active learning lets a learner choose which examples receive labels from a large unlabeled collection. This paper studies that choice for maximum likelihood estimation, broadening the theoretical focus beyond the PAC settings emphasized in earlier work. The objective is to fit a model while limiting the number of requested labels.

The authors propose a two-stage algorithm under conditions on the model class. Those conditions cover generalized linear models and encompass binary and multiclass classification, regression, and conditional random fields. The method therefore addresses a range of estimation tasks through one conditional theoretical framework.

An upper bound on the algorithm's label requirement matches a lower bound up to lower-order terms. This establishes near-optimal label use within the analyzed setting. A particularly useful consequence is that just one additional interaction round suffices for near-optimal maximum likelihood estimation. The abstract points to earlier empirical work on active linear and logistic regression as evidence of the approach's promise, rather than presenting that work as new experiments in this paper.
neurips-2015-convergence-rates-of-active.tldr: Under model-class conditions, a two-stage active learner achieves nearly optimal label requirements for maximum likelihood estimation.

paragraphs: Neural subunit models describe spike responses through two successive linear-nonlinear stages, with convolutional filters in the first stage. They offer a compact and biologically plausible account of early sensory responses. Fitting them is difficult, however, because likelihood evaluation is expensive and optimization encounters many local optima.

The paper connects these models to spike-triggered averages and covariances, statistics that summarize stimuli associated with spikes. A convolutional decomposition of those statistics yields an asymptotically efficient estimator under technical conditions. The authors also establish identifiability of the decomposition under mild assumptions, addressing whether its underlying components can be determined.

On neural recordings from macaque primary visual cortex, the moment-based methods outperform highly regularized GQM models. They also achieve predictive performance close to full maximum likelihood estimation at substantially lower computational cost. The significance is a connection between relatively accessible stimulus statistics and structured neural models, supported by conditional theory and a practical accuracy-versus-computation result on the studied recordings.
neurips-2015-convolutional-spike-trigger.tldr: Convolutional decomposition of spike-triggered statistics fits neural subunit models with conditional theoretical guarantees and near-likelihood predictive performance at lower cost.

paragraphs: An image combines information about an object with the effects of how it is viewed and illuminated. DC-IGN aims to separate these factors into an interpretable representation. Its goal is a graphics code whose components correspond to aspects of three-dimensional scenes and transformations such as pose and lighting.

The network uses multiple convolution and deconvolution layers and is trained with Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes. The authors introduce a training procedure that encourages particular code-layer neurons to represent particular transformations. This encouragement is central to making the representation controllable, rather than merely obtaining a compact description of an image.

Given one input image, the model can generate views of the same object with changed pose or lighting. The paper evaluates this ability qualitatively and quantitatively on object classes including faces and chairs. These tests examine whether the learned representation behaves like a rendering mechanism, connecting interpretable internal factors to visible changes in the generated images.
neurips-2015-deep-convolutional-inverse-.tldr: DC-IGN learns an image representation encouraged to separate pose and lighting, enabling new views of an object from one image.

paragraphs: Parallel deep learning must coordinate several workers without spending excessive time communicating. Elastic Averaging SGD connects each worker's parameters to a central parameter variable through an elastic force. Workers can move away from the center, allowing greater exploration while reducing communication with the parameter server.

The authors propose synchronous, asynchronous, and momentum-based versions. They analyze asynchronous stability under round-robin updates and give a simple sufficient condition for stability, contrasting this behavior with ADMM in their analysis. The round-robin setting and the stability condition are part of the guarantee, rather than an unconditional claim about every asynchronous execution.

Experiments suggest that additional exploration can improve deep learning performance in an optimization landscape with many local optima. The asynchronous method trains convolutional networks for image classification on CIFAR and ImageNet, accelerating training relative to DOWNPOUR and other common baselines while using communication efficiently. The contribution combines a concrete coordination mechanism with theoretical stability analysis and empirical evidence about training speed.
neurips-2015-deep-learning-with-elastic-.tldr: Elastic Averaging SGD lets parallel workers explore around shared parameters, achieving empirical training acceleration with efficient communication.

paragraphs: This paper builds a deep topic model for observations represented as counts. A Poisson distribution describes the observed count vectors, while a hierarchy of hidden binary units supplies multiple layers of latent structure. The architecture is assembled from Poisson Factor Analysis modules.

The key modeling choice is how to specify whether a hidden binary unit is active. Instead of a logistic function, the authors use a Bernoulli-Poisson link. That link enables repeated use of the same factor-analysis building blocks throughout the hierarchy. They also adapt the modules to construct discriminative topic models.

The paper derives both MCMC and stochastic variational inference methods. Their computation scales with nonzero entries in the data and binary units, giving efficiency advantages over models with logistic links. Experiments on several text corpora demonstrate advantages over related deep models. The approach ties its representational design to its computational design: the chosen link supports depth while making inference responsive to sparsity in the modeled quantities.
neurips-2015-deep-poisson-factor-modelin.tldr: A Bernoulli-Poisson link enables deep topic models built from reusable Poisson factor modules with efficient inference that scales with nonzero entries.

paragraphs: A useful feature representation must distinguish relevant classes while remaining robust to variation in the data. This balance matters especially when training examples are scarce. The paper presents a framework that explicitly trades the discriminative value of learned features against the learning algorithm's generalization error.

The method encourages the transformation from data to features to be a local isometry: it should preserve geometry in local neighborhoods. The authors show that this property improves a formal notion called (K, ε)-robustness. That result supplies a theoretical connection between the geometric behavior of the feature transformation and its ability to generalize.

The optimization framework can train standard learning models, including deep neural networks. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including Labeled Faces in the Wild, demonstrate the value of controlling the discrimination-robustness balance and show reductions in generalization error. The contribution is therefore both a training principle and a mathematical justification for encouraging a particular kind of geometry in learned features.
neurips-2015-discriminative-robust-trans.tldr: Encouraging feature transformations to preserve local geometry provides a principled way to balance discrimination and robustness.

paragraphs: Training samples provide an imperfect picture of the distribution a classifier will encounter. This paper models that uncertainty by placing a Wasserstein ball around the distribution that assigns equal weight to each training example. With an appropriately chosen radius, the ball contains the unknown generating distribution with high confidence.

The classifier minimizes expected logistic loss under the worst distribution inside that ball. Although this asks the learner to consider many possible distributions, the authors prove a tractable reformulation. The framework also includes ordinary and regularized logistic regression as special cases, connecting familiar objectives to distributional uncertainty.

The same Wasserstein construction produces upper and lower confidence bounds on the classifier's misclassification probability. Computing these bounds requires solving two tractable linear programs. Simulated and empirical experiments validate the stated out-of-sample guarantees. The approach thus addresses both choosing a classifier under uncertainty and quantifying its possible error, with the uncertainty radius playing a central role in the confidence claim.
neurips-2015-distributionally-robust-log.tldr: Wasserstein uncertainty sets yield tractable robust logistic regression and confidence bounds on classification error.

paragraphs: Compressive phase retrieval reconstructs a sparse vector using only the magnitudes of linear measurements. The difficulty combines missing phase information with sparsity. In matrix formulations, this creates a target that is both low rank and sparse, a combination that is difficult to recover through a general efficient convex method.

The paper changes how measurements are constructed. Sensing vectors are sampled randomly from an incoherent subspace, allowing the low-rank and sparse aspects of the recovery problem to be separated. Reconstruction then proceeds through two standard convex programs: first low-rank recovery, followed by sparse recovery.

Under this sensing construction, the authors show accurate estimation using O(k log(d/k)) measurements, where k is the number of nonzero signal entries and d is its dimension. They also evaluate the algorithm numerically. The result demonstrates how a deliberate restriction on measurement vectors can make a difficult combined structure manageable through sequential recovery methods, while retaining a favorable measurement requirement.
neurips-2015-efficient-compressive-phase.tldr: Structured random sensing separates low-rank and sparse recovery, enabling accurate compressive phase retrieval through two convex programs.

paragraphs: Galileo studies how visual observations can reveal physical properties and support predictions about future events. Its generative model places a three-dimensional physics engine at the center of scene understanding. Objects are represented through properties including mass, position, shape, and friction, which determine the simulations the engine produces.

The model infers hidden properties through relatively brief MCMC runs that drive simulations to fit important features of observed images and videos. The authors also explore a deep-learning route that maps visual inputs directly to physical properties. This reverses part of the generative process and provides another mechanism for inference.

Evaluation uses videos of simple scenes with rich physical behavior. Galileo infers object properties and predicts several kinds of physical events with accuracy comparable to human participants in those evaluations. The study supports a proposed account of vision in which generative physical knowledge plays a central role, with recognition models helping make inference efficient; it does not establish that account as a complete explanation of human vision.
neurips-2015-galileo-perceiving-physical.tldr: Galileo combines physical simulation and visual learning to infer object properties and predict events with human-comparable accuracy in its evaluated scenarios.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels can disagree because individual workers make mistakes. Learning from crowds therefore requires an aggregation rule that estimates the unknown true label from noisy responses. This paper introduces max-margin majority voting, or M³V, to improve how effectively aggregated votes distinguish competing labels.

The method encourages a margin between the score of a candidate true label and the scores of alternative labels. The authors then develop a Bayesian generalization that models noisy worker responses using worker confusion matrices. Joint learning becomes regularized Bayesian inference, with the margin requirement supplying the posterior regularization.

This construction combines discriminative separation with a generative account of worker errors. The resulting Bayesian model includes both M³V and the Dawid-Skene estimator, placing them within a shared framework. Empirical results show competitive performance, often exceeding state-of-the-art estimators in the reported evaluations. The contribution is a way to connect vote-based label separation with flexible modeling of how individual workers produce unreliable observations.
neurips-2015-max-margin-majority-voting-.tldr: Max-margin voting and a Bayesian extension combine stronger label separation with models of worker mistakes for crowdsourced annotation.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a hidden signal can be detected in a matrix of Gaussian noise. Under the signal hypothesis, a principal submatrix of size L has entries whose mean is shifted from zero to one, while their variance remains one. The task is to distinguish this case from pure noise.

For fixed positive ε, a hidden block of size (1 + ε)√n can be detected with probability approaching one by examining the largest eigenvalue. The authors prove that below (1 − ε)√n, no algorithm using only the matrix's eigenvalues can achieve error probability tending to zero. The restriction to eigenvalue information is essential to the scope of this impossibility result.

This boundary follows from a broader result about rank-one signals added to Gaussian tensors. There, the authors establish a lower bound on the critical signal-to-noise ratio needed for detection. The work therefore identifies a precise information bottleneck for spectral detection and connects it to a more general family of noisy signal problems.
neurips-2015-on-the-limitation-of-spectr.tldr: Below a hidden-block size of roughly √n, eigenvalue-only methods cannot detect a Gaussian hidden clique with vanishing error.

paragraphs: Variance-reduction methods improve stochastic gradient optimization by addressing variability in gradient updates. Algorithms such as SAG, SVRG, and SAGA had already shown theoretical and empirical advantages over ordinary SGD. This paper addresses their asynchronous use, an important issue when optimization must exploit parallel computing for large learning problems.

The authors introduce a common framework that captures multiple variance-reduction techniques. They then construct an asynchronous algorithm within it and establish fast convergence rates. Because the framework unifies several methods, asynchronous versions of SVRG and SAGA follow as consequences of the general approach.

The method achieves nearly linear speedup in sparse settings common in machine learning. Sparsity is therefore part of the stated context for this scaling result, rather than the claim applying to arbitrary data. An implementation of asynchronous SVRG provides empirical evidence. The contribution connects a family of statistical optimization improvements to parallel execution through shared analysis and a concrete working realization.
neurips-2015-on-variance-reduction-in-st.tldr: A unified variance-reduction framework yields asynchronous optimization algorithms with fast convergence and nearly linear speedup in sparse settings.

paragraphs: Binary prediction is often evaluated using the F-measure, which combines precision and recall. This is especially useful when class frequencies are imbalanced, a setting where simple error rate can be an inadequate guide. The paper takes that evaluation choice seriously by making F-measure maximization the learning objective.

Its focus is online learning, where learning proceeds as examples arrive. The authors propose an efficient online algorithm for optimizing the F-measure and formally analyze its convergence. This extends the question of learning for this metric into a sequential setting, connecting the algorithm's objective to the score used to judge its predictions.

Initial experiments show that the method performs well in practice. These empirical findings complement the convergence analysis: one addresses mathematical behavior, while the other provides early evidence of practical usefulness. The contribution is a metric-focused online learning method, motivated by the mismatch that can arise when a binary predictor is evaluated through precision and recall but trained with a simpler performance objective.
neurips-2015-online-f-measure-optimizati.tldr: An efficient online algorithm directly targets F-measure, with convergence analysis and encouraging initial experiments.

paragraphs: This paper considers predicting labels for graph vertices sequentially, using the vertices and labels observed so far. Its starting point is an Ising-model probability distribution built on the same graph. The ideal prediction selects the label with the largest marginal probability in the zero-temperature limit.

Computing those predictions involves a #P-complete problem, making direct use of the probabilistic rule computationally difficult. This motivates an efficient algorithm analyzed through online mistake bounds. Such guarantees address the errors accumulated over a sequence of predictions, matching the sequential nature of the task.

For trees, the algorithm is optimal and matches earlier results. On general graphs, it uses connectivity beyond that of a tree to obtain a bound expressed per cluster. Predicting all vertices takes cumulative time quadratic in graph size. The contribution thus connects a computationally demanding probabilistic prediction principle to an efficient sequential method whose guarantees reflect the graph's structure.
neurips-2015-online-prediction-at-the-li.tldr: An Ising-inspired online graph classifier provides mistake guarantees, tree optimality, and quadratic total prediction time.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can describe complex relationships, but operations on Gram matrices make them expensive for large datasets. Random Fourier features offer a computational alternative for shift-invariant kernels: replace the kernel with an easily computed, low-dimensional feature representation that supports fast linear algorithms.

This paper studies how accurately that replacement approximates the original kernel with a finite number of features. It establishes optimal guarantees in the uniform norm with respect to feature dimension and the size of an expanding approximation domain. It also gives guarantees in L^r norms for finite r, covering additional ways of measuring approximation error.

The authors extend the construction to derivatives of kernels and analyze their approximation quality as well. This matters because kernel-based tasks can involve derivatives as well as function values. The main contribution is theoretical control over a widely used computational shortcut: it explains how approximation quality scales and broadens that analysis to quantities beyond the kernel values themselves.
neurips-2015-optimal-rates-for-random-fo.tldr: The paper establishes finite-sample approximation guarantees for random Fourier features and extends the analysis to kernel derivatives.

paragraphs: Image segmentation assigns labels to individual pixels or locations in a volume. The paper contrasts the typically local context of fixed-input convolutional networks with multidimensional recurrent networks, which can gather context across an entire image or volume through a few sweeps. LSTM units make this recurrent approach particularly attractive.

The practical problem is parallel execution: earlier multidimensional LSTMs were difficult to run efficiently on GPUs. The authors reorganize the traditional cuboid computation order into a pyramidal arrangement. The resulting PyraMiD-LSTM is easier to parallelize, especially for three-dimensional inputs such as stacks of brain images.

PyraMiD-LSTM achieves the best known pixelwise brain-segmentation results reported by the paper on MRBrainS13 and competitive results on EM-ISBI12. These findings connect the computational reorganization to useful segmentation performance. The contribution makes broad-context recurrent processing more practical for volumetric biomedical imagery by changing the order of computation to expose parallel work.
neurips-2015-parallel-multi-dimensional-.tldr: PyraMiD-LSTM reorganizes multidimensional recurrence for GPU parallelism and achieves strong biomedical image-segmentation results.

paragraphs: Community recovery in the stochastic block model often assumes knowledge of model parameters or the number of communities. This paper develops efficient algorithms that dispense with that information while achieving optimal information-theoretic tradeoffs. Its guarantees differ according to how graph degrees scale.

In the constant-degree regime, the algorithm still needs a lower bound on relative community sizes and achieves optimal accuracy scaling for large degrees. When degrees diverge arbitrarily slowly, the community-size requirement can be removed and the model parameters learned efficiently. These distinctions specify what prior information is needed in each setting.

For logarithmic degrees, the authors obtain a fully agnostic algorithm that reaches the CH-limit for exact recovery in quasi-linear time. The results combine computational efficiency with optimal recovery guarantees across the stated regimes. Their significance is that unknown parameters need not prevent optimal community recovery, while the precise recovery objective and assumptions remain tied to graph density.
neurips-2015-recovering-communities-in-t.tldr: Efficient community-recovery algorithms attain optimal SBM tradeoffs without known parameters, with assumptions and guarantees depending on graph degree.

paragraphs: Partial monitoring models repeated decisions when the learner receives limited feedback about what happened. Each round pairs a chosen action with an outcome, producing both a loss and a feedback signal. This paper studies finite action sets and stochastic outcomes, with the aim of controlling accumulated regret.

The authors derive a logarithmic regret lower bound that depends on the outcome distribution. This describes problem difficulty more specifically than a single worst-case rate. They then introduce PM-DMED, inspired by a bandit algorithm, to pursue low distribution-dependent regret. Numerical experiments show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

For the matching theoretical guarantee, the authors modify PM-DMED using a hinge function. This variant, PM-DMED-Hinge, has an asymptotically optimal upper bound matching the lower bound. The distinction matters: the empirical performance claim concerns PM-DMED, while the stated optimality proof uses the modified algorithm. Together, the results supply a distribution-sensitive benchmark and an algorithm that asymptotically attains it.
neurips-2015-regret-lower-bound-and-opti.tldr: A distribution-dependent regret lower bound guides PM-DMED, whose hinge-modified variant asymptotically matches the bound.

paragraphs: An ensemble supplies several binary predictions for each example, creating an additional learning problem: how should those predictions be combined? This paper introduces an efficient algorithm that learns the aggregation. Its semi-supervised approach uses structure in the ensemble's predictions on unlabeled data to improve the combined result.

The method does not require assumptions about the ensemble's structure or where its classifiers came from. The authors also describe it as parameter-free and as scalable as linear learning. These properties make the aggregation procedure applicable without tailoring it to a particular way of constructing the ensemble.

Empirical evaluation with random forests demonstrates significant performance improvements. The central finding is that unlabeled examples can contribute useful information at the aggregation stage, through the pattern of predictions they elicit from the ensemble. The paper combines this empirical benefit with an efficient learning procedure, addressing the quality of the combined predictions and the computational practicality of learning how to combine them.
neurips-2015-scalable-semi-supervised-ag.tldr: A parameter-free aggregation algorithm uses ensemble predictions on unlabeled data to improve performance while scaling like linear learning.

paragraphs: Maximum a-posteriori inference seeks the most probable configuration in a model, but its standard form is a difficult combinatorial problem. Linear-programming relaxations provide useful approximations. Solving those relaxations can still be challenging because of nonsmoothness and constraints that couple different parts of the problem.

This paper studies adding a quadratic term to the relaxed objective to make it strongly convex. That changes the optimization problem, so the authors also bound how far the modified program's optimal value can lie from the original optimum. The analysis explicitly addresses the effect of introducing this additional curvature.

The authors develop suitable optimization algorithms and analyze their convergence, with linear convergence the focus identified in the title. The contribution links a modification intended to improve optimization behavior with guarantees on the resulting objective-value difference. This makes it possible to reason about computational progress and the consequences of changing the relaxation within the same mathematical framework.
neurips-2015-smooth-and-strong-map-infer.tldr: Adding a quadratic term to MAP relaxations provides strong convexity, analyzed optimization methods, and bounds on the change in optimal value.

paragraphs: Interactive submodular set cover studies how to choose inexpensive actions when the function to be satisfied is uncertain. The learner considers several hypotheses and seeks to bring all sufficiently plausible functions to a target value. Action costs matter, so the objective is to achieve coverage with as little cost-weighted action as possible.

The paper generalizes this setup by allowing each hypothesis to have a target determined by its plausibility. This smooth formulation makes the required level of satisfaction depend on the uncertainty attached to the hypothesis. It therefore extends the common-threshold version of the problem while retaining the action-selection objective.

The authors give the first algorithm for this generalized setting with theoretical optimality guarantees. They also extend the approach to real-valued functions, obtaining new theoretical results for both interactive and non-interactive submodular set cover. The contribution broadens how uncertainty and coverage requirements can be represented while preserving a framework for analyzing the quality of action choices.
neurips-2015-smooth-interactive-submodul.tldr: Smooth interactive submodular set cover lets coverage targets depend on hypothesis plausibility and provides algorithms with theoretical guarantees.
